operationalization: Use time-resolved tissue imaging to compare changes in organ-scale anisotropic growth with cell division orientation and topology. Competing causal models should predict whether tissue geometry precedes and explains cell-network organization or vice versa.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy studies can supply time-resolved cell segmentation and tissue geometry in selected model organisms.

obstacles: Causal direction is difficult to establish from observational imaging.
The claim spans plants and animals but data are concentrated in model systems.
rationale: The proposed variables are measurable, but 'overall configuration' and its causal priority require interpretation. Existing developmental imaging can test selected tissues, not the broad scope, and feedback between cell behavior and tissue form is a major confound.

operationalization: Classify mineral nucleation sites in histological and ultrastructural images by whether they lie inside metabolically active cytoplasm or in extracellular or inactive matrix. The generalization is supported if nucleation overwhelmingly occurs in matrix across representative calcifying and silicifying taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public cellular and ultrastructural image datasets may show mineral location relative to cells and matrix.

obstacles: Metabolic activity is rarely measured in the same images.
Public images are taxonomically and procedurally biased.
rationale: Mineral location is directly observable, but the active-versus-inactive distinction often needs proxy markers. Public microscopy can address particular tissues, while the cross-kingdom 'as a rule' scope would require extensive harmonization.

operationalization: Compare survival, developmental stage, skeletal-rod mineralization and arm length between control and calcium-depleted sea-urchin larvae. The claim is supported by viable stage-matched larvae lacking rods and long arms specifically under calcium depletion.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Searchable public study repository for experimental supplements and larval images.

obstacles: A dedicated open replication dataset may not exist.
Lime-free water can cause physiological effects beyond skeleton loss.
rationale: The treatment and outcomes give a clean experimental test with standard analysis. Public experimental records and images may test some species, but existence of sufficiently documented lime-free experiments is uncertain and the extension beyond echinoids is not covered.

operationalization: Combine measurements of marine circularly polarized sunlight with wavelength-specific asymmetric photolysis data for plausible prebiotic chiral compounds, then model whether the observed sign and magnitude could generate biological homochirality. Refutation would require showing the mechanism is absent or quantitatively insufficient under plausible early-Earth conditions.
obstacles: Early-Earth illumination and substrates are unobserved.
Present-day optical and laboratory data cannot identify a unique historical cause.
Many competing symmetry-breaking mechanisms make outcomes weakly discriminating.
rationale: The physical submechanism is testable, but the historical-origin claim requires substantial assumptions about unavailable initial conditions. Existing data could constrain plausibility but cannot resolve whether this process started biological homochirality.

operationalization: Quantify radial crystal orientation, concentric zoning, polymorph and organic-matrix distribution in images of pearls, otoliths and albumin-grown calcospherites. Shared multiscale structural signatures would support structural equivalence, but mechanism requires distinguishing common precipitation physics from other biomineralization routes.

candidate_datasets.name: Zenodo
candidate_datasets.role: Public repository containing microscopy and tomography datasets from biomineralization studies.

obstacles: Comparable raw images across all three materials are scattered.
Structural similarity alone does not establish identical formation mechanism.
rationale: Modern imaging makes the morphological comparison direct. Data are likely available piecemeal, but the mechanistic inference is underdetermined because similar zoning can arise through distinct matrix-controlled processes.

operationalization: For dated growth-zone series, test whether increments align reliably with independent seasonal or diel markers and compare externally forced versus endogenous reaction-diffusion models. Finding internally generated periodicity or poor alignment would refute the assumption that visible rings necessarily record external cycles.

candidate_datasets.name: PANGAEA
candidate_datasets.role: Public environmental and sclerochronological time-series data can link growth increments to external conditions.

obstacles: Different structures have different ring-forming mechanisms.
Environmental covariates and internal rhythms can be correlated.
rationale: The modest claim rejects necessity rather than all environmental control, so a single well-supported endogenous counterexample is informative. Open sclerochronology and environmental series can test several systems, though not the entire heterogeneous scope.

operationalization: Measure calcium carbonate and phosphate solubility and precipitation kinetics as intact albumins are enzymatically degraded, while controlling pH, carbonate and competing ions. Support requires protein breakdown to precede and quantitatively explain mineral precipitation better than direct acid-base chemistry.
obstacles: Public datasets rarely combine proteolysis kinetics with mineral supersaturation.
In vivo calcification includes active ion transport and specialized matrix proteins.
rationale: The chemical mechanism has measurable variables and experimentally separable rivals. However, suitable paired kinetic data appear unlikely to exist openly, and extrapolation from simplified solutions to all calcified tissues would remain inadequate.

operationalization: Across skeletal elements spanning orders of magnitude, estimate geometric scaling of surface, gravitational and loading stresses and compare form with predicted dominant-force regimes. Support requires a reproducible size transition from surface- or molecular-force signatures to load-adapted geometry.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D models provide skeletal geometry over a broad size and taxonomic range.

obstacles: Force dominance is inferred rather than directly observed.
Material composition, phylogeny and function covary with scale.
rationale: Scaling predictions are measurable, but 'molecular forces' is broad and requires modern reinterpretation. Morphological data support a comparative test, yet confounding and sparse microscopic taxa limit a clean general conclusion.

operationalization: Reconstruct the contemporaneous cell surface and spicule centerline in 3D, then test whether the centerline has near-zero geodesic curvature and fits the shortest surface path better than unconstrained growth models. Multiple developmental stages would test the proposed confinement mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
candidate_datasets.role: Open electron microscopy image archive that may include suitable sponge cellular ultrastructure.

obstacles: Adult spicules do not preserve the cell surface that constrained growth.
Matched developmental 3D images are rare.
rationale: Geodesicity has an explicit geometric test. Existing archives may contain spicule ultrastructure, but likely lack simultaneous high-resolution cell-surface reconstructions needed to resolve the mechanism.

operationalization: Extract quantitative shape descriptors for siliceous sponge and calcitic holothurian spicules and test convergence after controlling for developmental compartment geometry. Similar shapes across materials support material-independence only if within-material and cell-confinement alternatives are modeled.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public specimen scans may provide comparative spicule morphology.

obstacles: Similarity across materials does not by itself identify the shaping force.
Comparable developmental cell geometry is generally absent.
rationale: The morphological premise is testable with existing specimens and images. The conclusion that chemistry is irrelevant and confinement causal is weakly discriminated by morphology alone, so only part of the claim can be resolved.

operationalization: Measure ray angles and curvature in 3D spicules and, where developmental imaging exists, compare ray trajectories with three- and four-cell junctions. Support requires clustering near 120 and 109.47 degrees for equal-cell junctions and predictable deviations with unequal cells.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
candidate_datasets.role: Open volumetric electron microscopy can provide cellular junction and spicule geometry in selected specimens.

obstacles: Matched developing-cell and spicule datasets are scarce.
Crystal growth constraints can generate similar angles.
rationale: The angular predictions are precise and readily analyzed. Public morphology can test angle distributions, but resolving formation at cell junctions needs rare developmental volumes and controls for crystallography.

operationalization: Reconstruct vesicle centers and nascent six-rayed spicules in developing hexactinellids, classify packing as cubic or close-packed, and test whether ray axes follow cubic nearest-neighbor directions. A close-packed arrangement with unchanged spicule geometry would refute the mechanism.
obstacles: Developmental 3D data for glass sponges are exceptionally scarce.
Mature skeletons cannot uniquely recover prior vesicle packing.
rationale: The packing mechanism makes a clear geometric prediction. Existing specimen data can show six-rayed geometry but are unlikely to contain the developmental vesicle arrangement required for a discriminating test.

operationalization: Estimate species range sizes, occupancy, local richness, dominance and fossil first occurrences from georeferenced living and fossil records, with standardized sampling and taxonomic validation. The claim predicts unusually broad ranges, high local richness, weak dominance and long genus or family durations.

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: Public georeferenced occurrence records for living marine Radiolaria.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrences for evaluating temporal ranges and ancient records.

obstacles: Micropaleontological taxonomy has substantial synonymy and revision.
Sampling effort is highly uneven in space, depth and geological time.
rationale: Distribution and assemblage claims map directly to occurrence records, and large open databases exist. Biases and incomplete identification weaken global and Cambrian-era conclusions, but major parts are presently testable.

operationalization: Relate particle incorporation probabilities to particle size, shape, chemistry and measured interfacial energies in time-lapse observations of shell building. A surface-energy model must predict selectivity and assembly without organismal transport behavior better than active-choice models.
obstacles: Surface energy is not usually measured alongside particle-selection behavior.
Active cytoskeletal transport and passive trapping can coexist.
rationale: The mechanism can be formalized, but 'purely physical' requires excluding active biological processes. Existing images of agglutinated tests lack the simultaneous behavioral and interfacial measurements needed for that discrimination.

operationalization: Co-register developing vesicle boundaries and silica deposition in 3D and quantify whether rods arise specifically in intervesicular grooves, with mesh regularity tracking vesicle size variance and layers tracking repeated vesicle shells. Alternative cytoskeletal templates should be compared.

candidate_datasets.name: EMPIAR
candidate_datasets.role: Potential source of open ultrastructural volumes for protist silicification.

obstacles: Suitable live or staged radiolarian ultrastructure is rare.
Adult lattice geometry does not uniquely reveal the deposition template.
rationale: The mechanism gives clear spatial and correlational predictions. Public imaging may describe mature shells, but matched developmental vesicle and silica maps across the named taxa are unlikely to be adequate.

operationalization: Compare lattice regularity and topology across silica-, celestite- and organic-skeleton taxa using standardized images, then test whether material predicts form after phylogeny and size are controlled. Demonstrating an underlying vesicular template requires direct developmental imaging rather than cross-material convergence alone.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D media for comparing skeletal lattice geometry across specimens.

obstacles: Cross-material convergence is not unique evidence for vesicle moulding.
The groups differ in phylogeny, ecology and scale.
rationale: Material-independence of gross form is measurable from existing morphology. The stronger causal inference to an underlying vesicular structure remains poorly discriminated without developmental observations.

operationalization: Reconstruct Callimitra skeletons and developing cells in 3D, testing for six interfaces, triple junctions near 120 degrees and tetrahedral edge angles near 109.47 degrees with direct colocalization at cell boundaries. Development without four-cell contact would refute the asserted necessity.
obstacles: Modern developmental imaging of Callimitra is likely absent.
A tetrahedral skeleton can arise from non-cellular geometric processes.
rationale: The geometry is precise, but mature shape alone cannot establish where it formed. The necessary developmental cellular context is too specialized to expect adequate public data.

operationalization: Measure face, edge and angle equality in 3D polyhedral radiolarian specimens to determine whether regular dodecahedra and icosahedra truly occur. If regularity is confirmed, compare the structure with crystallographic periodic tessellation predictions, while distinguishing crystal lattice formation from broader space-partitioning mechanisms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D specimen data can test whether purported polyhedra are geometrically regular.

obstacles: Haeckel's drawings may idealize specimen geometry.
Noncrystallographic dodecahedra do not exclude every space-partitioning process.
rationale: Modern geometry can test the critical descriptive premise and periodic crystals indeed constrain rotational symmetry. Available 3D coverage is uncertain, and the broader mechanistic exclusion is less direct than the morphological test.

operationalization: Digitize 3D spine directions in twenty-spined specimens and fit the hexagonal 2+6+6+6 arrangement against Müller's five four-spined circles using angular residuals. Taxon-level model support would directly confirm which arrangement applies.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D models may permit direct measurement of radial-spine arrangements.

obstacles: Suitable intact microscopic 3D specimens may be sparse.
The assertion that Müller's pattern fits no case requires broad taxonomic coverage.
rationale: The rival arrangements make precise, mutually distinguishable predictions and analysis is straightforward once 3D data exist. Public coverage can likely test examples but not the universal rejection across all relevant taxa.

operationalization: In developing Radiolaria, temporally map polarity markers, central cytoplasmic organization, peripheral vesicles and nascent spines, then perturb candidate central and peripheral mechanisms. The claim predicts central polarity before spine placement and persistence when peripheral mechanics are altered.
obstacles: The proposed 'directive forces' have no unique modern observable.
Developmental perturbation data for these organisms are lacking.
Absence of an obvious peripheral mechanism is not evidence for a central force.
rationale: A modernized central-versus-peripheral origin can be tested, but Thompson's positive force concept is underspecified. Existing mature morphology cannot establish temporal or causal origin, making new developmental data necessary.

operationalization: Fit centerlines of annular, longitudinal and helical wall thickenings to geodesics on reconstructed cylindrical cell, vessel and tracheal surfaces. Support requires low geodesic curvature compared with plausible nongeodesic curves across the named structures.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open microscopy datasets can supply 3D plant vascular and insect tracheal geometry.

obstacles: Real biological tubes depart from ideal cylinders.
Pattern classes may be visually described without enough resolution for geodesic fitting.
rationale: The geometric criterion is explicit and standard image analysis is feasible. Existing images can test representative structures, though cross-taxon coverage and deviations from cylindrical geometry limit the full generalization.

operationalization: Reconstruct high-spired shells, model the local shell envelope as a cone and compare the sutural and parallel striation paths with calculated surface geodesics. The claim is supported if their geodesic residuals are low and coil spacing decreases toward the apex as predicted.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D gastropod shell models allow cone fitting and geodesic-path analysis.

obstacles: Shell surfaces are only approximately conical.
Erosion or ornament can obscure sutures and striations.
rationale: This is a precise geometric statement testable from existing 3D shell scans with standard methods. Broad enough Turritella and related material is publicly represented to confirm or refute the principal claim.

operationalization: On 3D curved biological surfaces, extract crossing line systems and test each family for low geodesic curvature, then estimate how often reticulation is generated by two such families rather than branching or cellular tiling. A representative prevalence estimate would address the phrase 'very common.'

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public microscopy offers examples of reticulated patterns on biological surfaces.

obstacles: The scope and threshold for 'very common' are unspecified.
Many reticula arise through branching networks or cell packing.
rationale: Individual cases can be tested geometrically, but the frequency claim requires defining a sampling universe and compiling diverse structures. Open images support restricted tests rather than a decisive general prevalence estimate.

operationalization: Map muscle-fibre trajectories onto 3D organ surfaces and compute geodesic curvature and path length relative to endpoint-matched shortest paths. Developmental or mechanical data must additionally test whether tension causes alignment rather than merely correlating with it.

candidate_datasets.name: HuBMAP Data Portal
candidate_datasets.role: Open spatial imaging and tissue maps for human hollow organs.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Public 3D microscopy from model organisms can provide fibre orientation.

obstacles: Anatomical fibre tracts often have changing insertion points and layered helices.
Geodesic alignment does not prove automatic tension-driven arrangement.
rationale: Fibre geometry is measurable in modern 3D datasets, and representative organs can be analyzed quickly. The causal 'automatically' mechanism and broad organ scope remain confounded by development and function.

operationalization: Register embryonic heart and stomach tube stages to later organ surfaces, track fibre lineages, and test whether trajectories remain geodesic after deformation and whether shorter paths predict contraction efficiency. Compare with active fibre-remodeling models.

candidate_datasets.name: eMouseAtlas
candidate_datasets.role: Public mouse developmental anatomy and gene-expression resources for organ morphogenesis.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Open developmental imaging may provide fibre and surface geometry.

obstacles: Lineage-resolved fibre tracking across twisting stages is uncommon.
Fibres differentiate and remodel during organogenesis rather than simply deforming passively.
rationale: Parts of the geometry can be tested in developmental atlases, but 'remain geodetic' requires longitudinal correspondence rarely present. Efficiency and persistence claims have multiple developmental and biomechanical rivals.

operationalization: Track 3D position and body orientation of swimming microorganisms, estimating axial rotation, body-fixed curvature and helix pitch. The mechanism is supported when observed trajectories follow parameters predicted from rotation and swerve and become circular when rotation approaches zero.

candidate_datasets.name: BioStudies
candidate_datasets.role: Public supplementary microscopy videos can provide organism trajectories and body orientation.

obstacles: Many videos are two-dimensional.
Phototaxis, boundaries and fluid flow can perturb paths.
rationale: The kinematic mechanism has precise and discriminating predictions, and published open videos cover multiple ciliated and flagellated swimmers. Standard tracking can resolve the core claim, though not every taxon in its broad scope.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic and alternative spiral models to digitized horns, shell trajectories, foraminiferal coils and sunflower parastichies, using out-of-sample residuals and parameter constancy. The universal claim is refuted by robust nonlogarithmic examples within any included class.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D scans of horns, shells and foraminifera for curve fitting.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Public images provide broad examples of sunflower heads and external biological spirals.

obstacles: Perspective and sectioning can distort fitted spirals.
Sunflower phyllotaxis is a point pattern rather than a single permanent curve.
rationale: The claimed universality and named exception are directly falsifiable with abundant public morphology. Standard model comparison can determine whether logarithmic spirals fit better than Archimedean or variable-pitch alternatives.

operationalization: Model and compare growing structures under fixed laboratory-frame versus body-rotating deflection fields, then test whether shell growth orientation and columellar-muscle geometry predict the observed spiral. A stable spiral under a demonstrably external fixed-direction force would refute necessity.
obstacles: Growth-force direction is rarely measured in existing datasets.
Multiple intrinsic growth asymmetries can mimic muscle deflection.
The mathematical necessity depends on idealized force assumptions.
rationale: The fixed-versus-body-frame distinction is formalizable, but morphology alone cannot recover force direction. Existing shell scans are inadequate to identify the proposed columellar-muscle mechanism without new developmental or mechanical measurements.

operationalization: Estimate local longitudinal and transverse accretion rates from successive growth increments and test whether their ratio is constant and predicts a constant-angle logarithmic centerline. Variable ratios should predict systematic departures from logarithmic form.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shells and horns preserve successive accretion geometry for growth-ratio estimation.

obstacles: Static growth lines are proxies for rates.
Tube cross-section and torsion can complicate the ideal model.
rationale: The claim supplies a quantitative relation between measurable ratios and spiral angle. Existing accretionary hard parts retain growth histories, allowing standard geometric tests across representative shells and horns.

operationalization: Digitize shoot origins, angles and lengths in scorpioid and helicoid cymes and test constancy of angle and length ratio, then fit the shoot tangents to logarithmic versus alternative spirals. Three-dimensional reconstruction can remove the superimposed helicoid twist.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Public plant photographs provide broad but mostly 2D observations of cymose inflorescences.

obstacles: Photographs often have perspective distortion and hidden shoots.
Successive lengths may vary with flowering stage and environment.
rationale: The mathematical conditions and curve fit are explicit. Public imagery can test visible scorpioid examples, while reliable 3D data for hidden helicoid geometry and representative taxonomic coverage are limited.

operationalization: Segment successive growth stages preserved by whorls or growth lines, rescale them and quantify shape similarity, terminal accretion and logarithmic-spiral fit. Systematic ontogenetic parameter change or a nonlogarithmic self-similar curve would refute the stated biological or uniqueness component.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell and horn scans preserve ontogenetic increments for similarity analysis.

obstacles: Shell ornament and damage affect registration.
The mathematical uniqueness statement depends on the precise definition of spiral and similarity.
rationale: Self-similarity and accretion geometry are direct measurements from abundant scans. Both biological constancy and the logarithmic model can be compared quantitatively against alternatives with standard methods.

operationalization: Partition accretionary structures at successive growth boundaries and test whether adding each increment produces a whole geometrically similar to the prior whole under one scale transformation. Deviations can be quantified by registered shape residuals.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D scans of shells, horns and tusks allow gnomon and similarity tests.

obstacles: Growth boundaries may be incomplete or obscured.
Foraminiferal chambers can change shape during ontogeny.
rationale: The gnomon property has a direct geometric criterion and accretionary records are widely preserved. Existing 3D data can confirm or refute it across several named structure classes, though the word 'all' remains demanding.

operationalization: Sample curves from simultaneously formed soft outlines and incrementally accreted hard parts, fit logarithmic and rival models, and test association between accretion mode, logarithmic fit and visible growth lines. Credible logarithmic soft-tissue counterexamples would refute the exclusion.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D media for accretionary hard-part curves.

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: Large public image source for leaf margins, fish contours, claws and horns.

obstacles: Determining whether a part is formed simultaneously may require developmental knowledge.
Curve fitting is sensitive to landmark and scale selection.
rationale: The prediction contrasts observable structure classes and can be falsified by public morphology. Coverage is broad enough for a strong comparative test, although developmental mode must sometimes be assigned from external knowledge.

operationalization: Measure successive whorl breadths along homologous radii and test whether their ratios are constant, including whether Nautilus is near three. Compare geometric-progression residuals across nautiloids, ammonoids and gastropods.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D and sectional shell models allow direct whorl-breadth measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil metadata can support broad taxonomic sampling of ammonoids and nautiloids.

obstacles: Fossil deformation can alter whorl dimensions.
Species and ontogenetic stage sampling may be uneven.
rationale: This is an unusually direct quantitative claim with abundant preserved specimens and a clear refuting result. Standard morphometrics can evaluate both Nautilus's stated ratio and the broader generalization.

operationalization: Fit a generative shell model parameterizing aperture shape, expansion, rotation, translation and inclination to diverse univalve scans, then quantify unexplained shape variance and systematic residuals. The claim is supported if this parameter set reconstructs observed forms without additional qualitative mechanisms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Large open collection of 3D molluscan shell morphology for generative-model fitting.

obstacles: Ornament, aperture remodeling and local growth changes exceed the simple parameter set.
A flexible model can fit shapes without identifying biological causation.
rationale: Modern shell models make the proposed factors measurable and public scans offer broad coverage. The universal 'all differences' assertion and causal sufficiency are harder to discriminate because model flexibility and omitted ornament matter.

operationalization: Fit logarithmic spirals to shell whorls and estimate constant angles with uncertainty for Nautilus, ammonitoids and gastropods. Test Nautilus against about 80 degrees and estimate the fraction of ordinary taxa inside 80–85 degrees or below 80 degrees.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell scans enable direct estimation of spiral angles.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrence and taxonomy support representative ammonoid sampling.

obstacles: The terms 'ordinary' and 'typical' require a sampling definition.
Diagenetic deformation biases fossil measurements.
rationale: The numerical range is directly measurable from abundant living and fossil shells. Standard curve fitting and representative sampling can strongly confirm or refute the stated distribution.

operationalization: Estimate outer- and inner-border growth increments from shell growth geometry and regress whorl separation, contact and overlap against their ratio. Test whether other parameters such as aperture shape and translation improve prediction beyond that ratio.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell scans provide whorl overlap and border-growth geometry.

obstacles: Static geometry only indirectly estimates growth rates.
Several shell-model parameters can affect apparent overlap.
rationale: The predicted association is quantitatively testable from existing scans. The word 'only' demands exclusion of correlated geometric factors, and inferred rates make that causal sufficiency less clean.

operationalization: Using independently inferred cephalopod phylogenies and stratigraphy, test whether spiral angle alone predicts ancestor-descendant order or primitiveness after accounting for size and clade. Frequent convergence and poor temporal prediction would support the warning against inference from angle alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil occurrences and ages for testing temporal order of shell forms.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open shell morphology for spiral-angle measurements.

obstacles: Independent fossil phylogenies remain uncertain.
The phrase 'no valid evidence' is methodological rather than a simple empirical frequency claim.
rationale: Existing fossil and morphology data can quantify how informative spiral angle is about age and descent. They cannot prove that angle provides no evidence in every model, but can resolve the historical series and convergence components.

operationalization: Estimate shell growth parameters along independently inferred lineages and test for sustained directional trends, while measuring homoplasy of similar parameter combinations across distant clades. Compare detection against qualitative morphology alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil chronology and taxonomy for directional-trend analyses.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell data for quantitative growth parameters.

obstacles: Orthogenesis has multiple historical and modern meanings.
Directional trends may reflect sampling, selection or phylogenetic structure.
Independent phylogenies are incomplete for many fossil series.
rationale: Directional parameter change and convergence are measurable with public fossil morphology. The broad claim about what mathematical morphology can reveal is partly methodological, and attributing trends to orthogenesis requires substantial interpretation.

operationalization: Measure local spiral angle and whorl breadth through ontogeny in the named ammonoids and test whether increasing angle predicts narrowing while decline toward zero predicts uncoiling. Alternative local curve models provide direct comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open fossil shell scans preserve ontogenetic coiling trajectories.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public taxonomy and occurrences help identify and sample the named ammonoid groups.

obstacles: Fossil crushing can distort local angles.
Some named historical taxa have revised classifications.
rationale: The claim makes explicit within-shell quantitative predictions and fossils preserve the relevant trajectory. Existing scans and standard curve analysis can resolve the pattern in the named forms.

operationalization: Estimate spiral and apical angles from 3D specimens of Cerithium, Solarium, Natica and Planorbis, then partition intergeneric shape variance attributable to each. The claim predicts low variation in spiral angle and dominant variation in apical angle.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D gastropod shell models enable direct angle and variance measurements.

obstacles: Within-genus species variation requires balanced sampling.
Aperture shape and ornament add differences not represented by the two angles.
rationale: Both quantities are directly measurable and the named common shell groups are represented in public collections. Variance decomposition gives a clear test of the comparative statement.

operationalization: Digitize successive growth lines on bivalve and brachiopod shells, test whether they share an umbonal axis, and fit circular, elliptical and direction-dependent growth models. Directional increment rates should quantitatively generate the observed line family.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open 3D shell surfaces allow extraction and fitting of growth lines.

obstacles: Fine growth lines may be below scan resolution.
Environmental interruptions can perturb otherwise regular line families.
rationale: The claim connects visible curves to explicit geometric growth models. Existing shell media can resolve the major pattern and named form differences using routine morphometrics.

operationalization: Use developmental imaging and preserved carapaces to test whether successive retained exuviae adhere as nested layers, project beyond prior margins and generate fitted logarithmic growth lines. Comparison with fully moulting branchiopods would test the incomplete-moult mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Public micro-CT data may reveal nested carapace layers and external growth lines.

candidate_datasets.name: BioImage Archive
candidate_datasets.role: Potential open developmental microscopy of branchiopod moulting.

obstacles: Estheria is a historical taxonomic name.
Static carapaces may not distinguish retained moults from continuous secretion.
rationale: Nested layers and spiral lines are measurable, and the mechanism has a useful comparative prediction. Public developmental coverage of the relevant clam-shrimp taxa is likely too sparse for full causal resolution.

operationalization: Reconstruct shell interior and brachidium geometry across spire-bearing brachiopods, quantify shell elongation and flattening, and test the predicted association with outward, inward or discoid spiral direction. Phylogenetically controlled models should compare spatial constraint with clade-specific development.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open micro-CT models can preserve internal brachidia and external shell shape.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public fossil taxonomy and occurrences support sampling across brachiopod groups.

obstacles: Internal brachidia are incompletely preserved.
Shell shape and arm direction are strongly confounded with phylogeny.
rationale: The association is directly testable with fossil 3D morphology, including the named form classes. Demonstrating that pressure and available space cause the pattern is less discriminating than documenting the predicted correlation.

operationalization: Combine fossil positional evidence, microstructure and independent cephalopod phylogenies to test homology between ammonite aptychi and dorsal shell components, and compare developmental boundary predictions from a split-cone model. Support requires congruent tissue homology and ancestral-state reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Public ammonoid fossil occurrences and taxonomy for historical reconstruction.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open cephalopod fossil and shell scans for structural comparison.

obstacles: Soft-tissue attachment and embryonic stages are rarely preserved.
Deep homology alternatives can fit fragmentary fossil evidence.
The once-united ancestral structure is not directly observable.
rationale: Modern fossil and comparative data can test several consequences and likely reject or support homology hypotheses. The exact ancestral split event is a historical inference with incomplete preservation, preventing full resolution.

operationalization: Extract septal surfaces and attachment boundaries from 3D shells, solve the corresponding minimal-surface problem, and compare observed curvature and area with minimal, constant-mean-curvature and biomechanical alternatives. Shape classes should track boundary orientation as predicted.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open micro-CT shell volumes reveal internal cephalopod septa and attachment lines.

obstacles: Uniform pressure and isotropic membrane assumptions are not directly recorded.
Fossil deformation and later calcification can alter original septal shape.
rationale: Modern CT and numerical geometry permit a direct comparison of observed septa with boundary-matched surfaces. Mechanistic assumptions are not perfectly recoverable, but the core minimal-surface prediction is resolvable from existing data.

operationalization: Quantify branch topology, tip curvature and wavelength in ammonitic sutures and compare them with explicit surface-tension instability models and rival growth or buckling models. A surface-tension account must uniquely reproduce scaling and branching statistics, not merely visual resemblance.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open ammonite scans provide complex suture geometry.

obstacles: Pattern resemblance is non-unique across physical mechanisms.
Interfacial tensions during septum formation are not preserved.
Many fossils expose only 2D suture traces.
rationale: Suture morphology is abundant and measurable, but the analogical mechanism is weakly discriminating because reaction-diffusion, differential growth and buckling can produce similar branching. Existing data can test model fit, not confidently identify surface tension as the cause.

operationalization: Parameterize spiral shell form across molluscs, foraminifera and tube worms, then model recurrence and convergence against phylogeny, geological age, climate, depth and geography. The claim predicts frequent cross-group near-identity and weak environmental or temporal structure.

obstacles: Morphology and occurrence databases require substantial taxonomic linkage.
Preservation and collecting biases vary strongly through time and habitat.
Claims about 'every' period and sea exceed actual coverage.
rationale: Large open fossil, occurrence and morphology resources address all major variables. They can test recurrence and environmental association broadly, but harmonization and severe sampling biases prevent literal resolution of the universal scope.

operationalization: Compare generative growth-only models and selection-aware evolutionary models against shell-form distributions, fitness proxies and phylogenetic transitions. Growth laws explain possibility, while evidence that form affects survival or reproduction would refute the strongest claim of no selective share.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Open quantitative shell morphology for evolutionary model comparison.

obstacles: 'No necessary share' is a modal claim and cannot be proved by observational fit.
Growth constraints and natural selection are compatible rather than exclusive.
Fossil occurrence is an imperfect fitness proxy.
rationale: Existing data can test whether selection is associated with shell form and whether growth laws generate observed possibilities. They cannot resolve the non-necessity formulation cleanly, because a physical growth mechanism does not exclude evolutionary selection on its parameters.
